hook.text: In 1995, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone after 70 years of absence.

buildup.text: Without wolves, elk overgrazed riverbanks. Trees vanished. Riverbanks eroded badly.

discovery.text: Wolves kept elk moving. Willow and aspen trees returned along the streams.

twist.text: Roots stabilized banks. Rivers narrowed and deepened. Even the shape of waterways changed.

climax.text: Beavers, songbirds, and fish all returned. Wolves had triggered a trophic cascade.

punchline.text: Wolves didn't just change the animals. They changed the rivers.

quiz.question: What is a trophic cascade?
options: A chain reaction through an ecosystem triggered by a top predator
A disease that spreads between species

details.summary: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 after a 70-year absence, triggering a trophic cascade that restored riverbanks, recovered beaver populations, and increased biodiversity across the ecosystem.
details.whyItMatters: Yellowstone's wolves are the most famous example of how restoring a single predator can heal an entire landscape. The story reshaped conservation thinking worldwide.
takeaways: Wolf removal caused elk overpopulation and riverbank erosion
Reintroduction allowed willows and aspens to regrow along rivers
Beavers, songbirds, and fish populations recovered as habitat improved

faq.question: How did wolves change the rivers of Yellowstone?
faq.answer: Wolves reduced elk browsing along riverbanks, allowing willow and aspen to regrow. Stronger root systems stabilized banks, reducing erosion. Beavers returned to build dams, creating pools that supported fish, amphibians, and waterfowl.

faq.question: Did Yellowstone's wolves affect every species in the park?
faq.answer: The effects were widespread but complex. Scavengers like ravens and bears benefited from wolf kills. Some prey species declined while vegetation and dependent species recovered. The net effect was increased overall biodiversity.
